article.Citation: Schenberg EE, et al. Treating drug dependence with the aid of ibogaine: A retrospective study. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2014.
article.Title: Treating drug dependence with the aid of ibogaine: A retrospective study

ae_events.Description: Nausea during acute ibogaine effects (~10hr session); author-labeled a mild adverse effect, occurred frequently.
Ataxia during acute ibogaine effects; author-labeled mild; discussion notes absence of persistent ataxia.
Vomiting during acute ibogaine effects; author-labeled a mild adverse effect, occurred frequently.
Tremors during acute ibogaine effects; author-labeled a mild adverse effect, occurred frequently.
Headaches during acute ibogaine effects; author-labeled a mild adverse effect, occurred frequently.
Mental confusion during acute ibogaine effects; author-labeled a mild adverse effect, occurred frequently.
4 patients (5%) complained about the psychotherapeutic process/clinic activities during internment or post-ibogaine sessions.

article.PosResult: Authors report 61% overall abstinence, a statistically significant (p<0.001) increase in abstinence duration after ibogaine vs. before, and conclude in both the abstract and discussion that ibogaine "can be a safe and effective treatment" for stimulant/non-opiate drug dependence, meeting the study's own definition of a positive result.
article.IsObservational: Retrospective chart/interview review of a private clinic's real-world ibogaine treatment as delivered in usual (non-research) practice; no randomization, no comparator arm, no research-only interventional protocol -- observational cohort/case-series design.
article.Condition: Study population is poly-substance dependent (64% lifetime alcohol, 81% cannabis, 83% cocaine, 68% crack; 72% poly-drug users) with the paper's own framing as a stimulant/non-opioid dependence study (only 1 of 75 patients had opioid history, tobacco used by 15% but not a treatment target). Does not cleanly map to Alcohol, Smoking, or Opioid, so coded '.' per the indeterminate-case instruction.
article.N: 75 patients had data gathered and are the basis for the core sample-level results (drug-use history, sessions, adverse reactions); some downstream sub-analyses (e.g., abstinence-duration comparisons) use smaller subsamples (n=66, n=41, etc.) due to incomplete follow-up data, but N=75 is the overall analyzed cohort.
article.AE_denominator: Not explicitly restated as a distinct AE-assessment population; inferred as 75 because the reported '4 patients (5%)' complaint figure is consistent with a denominator of 75 (4/75=5.3%).
article.PctBIPOC: Article reports no race/ethnicity data for the sample.
article.PctIndigenous: Article reports no race/ethnicity data for the sample.
article.NumDistinctAEs: Counted as 7 distinct types: nausea, ataxia, vomiting, tremors, headache, mental confusion (all explicitly grouped by authors as 'mild adverse effects' occurring during acute ibogaine effects), plus a 7th, qualitatively different category -- 4 patients (5%) who complained about the psychotherapeutic process/clinic activities. This 7th category is not a pharmacological/physiological AE and its inclusion is a borderline call; included per the safety-dataset instruction to avoid understating harm/complaints, flagged here for reviewer judgment.
article.NParticipantsWithAE: No single overall participant-with-AE count is given. The six acute physical AEs are described only as occurring 'frequently' with no per-event participant counts; only the psychotherapeutic-process complaint category has an explicit count (4 patients, 5%), so an aggregate figure cannot be reliably constructed without double-counting risk.
article.ArmScope: Single-arm retrospective cohort/case series -- all 75 patients received ibogaine, no non-exposed comparator group -- so ArmScope is psychedelic_arm per the instruction that single-arm case series/cohorts default to this value.

ae_events.Schenberg 2014_AE01: Authors explicitly describe nausea, ataxia, vomiting, tremors, headaches, and mental confusion as 'mild adverse effects' occurring 'only during the acute effects of ibogaine' -- author-assigned severity label used (SeveritySource=author) rather than the rubric default.
ae_events.Schenberg 2014_AE02: Same author-labeled 'mild' grouping as AE01; discussion section separately notes absence of persistent ataxia, supporting transient/Mild classification.
ae_events.Schenberg 2014_AE07: Reported with minimal detail (no description of what was intervened, whether resolved, or functional impact) -- graded Mild by rubric default with SeverityIndeterminate=Y. Onset marked 'unknown' because the article gives an ambiguous timeframe ('during the internment period ... or during the post-ibogaine psychotherapeutic sessions'), spanning both the residential stay and ongoing post-treatment therapy. InterventionRequired coded '.' since no information is given on whether any response/intervention followed these complaints.
